lessons.title: Lower or Nil TDS Certificates: When and How to Apply

body.text: When your real tax is far below the TDS being cut, and Form 121 is not an option, you can ask the tax officer to fix a lower rate in advance. A certificate under Section 395 tells your payers exactly how much to deduct, so your cash stays with you instead of waiting as a refund.

children.text: Dr Farah, 45, is a consultant radiologist in Bengaluru who reports for three private hospitals. Her fees for tax year 2026-27 will be about ₹48,00,000, and every hospital deducts 10% TDS: ₹4,80,000 a year. Under presumptive taxation her actual tax is ₹3,12,000. That leaves ₹1,68,000 of her own money sitting with the government until her refund arrives, often late in the following year. Her tax is not nil, so Form 121 is out. This lesson covers the tool built for exactly her situation.

markDefs.definition: A certificate issued by the Assessing Officer under Section 395 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (formerly Section 197), directing a named payer to deduct TDS at a specified lower rate, or not at all, up to a specified amount for a tax year.

children.text: Chapter 4 has two ways to reduce TDS before it happens. You met the first, Form 121, in Lesson 1. The second is a
under Section 395(1) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (formerly Section 197). You apply online using Form 128 (formerly Form 13).

columns.label: Form 121 (Section 393(6))
points: Resident individuals, HUFs and similar persons only
Only when tax for the year is nil, plus an income cap below 60
Given directly to each payer, takes effect immediately
Mainly interest, dividends, EPF and similar income

columns.label: Certificate (Section 395)
points: Anyone, including non-residents, firms and companies
When estimated income justifies a lower rate or nil
Applied for online, typically decided within about 30 days
Covers a wide range of TDS, including professional fees, rent and payments to non-residents

cells: Professionals and freelancers with large receipts
10% TDS on gross fees, while tax is computed on profit after expenses or presumptive income
Their tax is reduced, not nil
Individuals below 60 with nil tax but large interest income
10% TDS on interest above ₹50,000, although the rebate makes their tax nil
Declared income above the ₹4,00,000 Form 121 cap
Non-residents selling property in India
TDS on capital gains, often calculated on the whole sale price
Non-residents cannot use Form 121
Businesses with brought-forward losses
TDS on receipts while current-year profit is absorbed by old losses
Not individuals, or tax not nil

children.text: Megha from Lesson 1, who earns ₹5,50,000 of FD interest with nil tax but was turned away on Form 121, is a textbook case. A nil deduction certificate addressed to her bank would stop the ₹55,000 of TDS that Form 121 could not.

body.caption: Why she qualifies for a lower rate

cells: Expected fees from three hospitals
Presumptive income at 50% of receipts
Tax in the new regime, with 4% cess
TDS at 10% without a certificate
Excess locked up until refund
Her actual tax as a share of fees

body.title: Dr Farah: TDS vs actual tax for the year
Try It: The Rate an Officer Might Set
body.prompt: If the Assessing Officer accepts Dr Farah's estimate of ₹3,12,000 tax on ₹48,00,000 of fees, what lower TDS rate would make her TDS roughly match her tax? Answer as a percentage.
body.explanation: ₹3,12,000 divided by ₹48,00,000 is 6.5%. In practice the officer also looks at her past returns, any tax already paid or outstanding, and her other income, so the rate on the certificate may differ. But the logic is to align TDS with the tax she is actually expected to owe.

cells: 1. Prepare an estimate
Work out your expected income and tax for the tax year, and list each payer with its TAN and the amount you expect to receive from it
2. Gather support
Keep returns for the last three years, recent financial statements or income computations, and details of TDS already deducted this year
3. File Form 128 online
Apply through the TRACES system with your PAN. Applications for payments to non-residents need details of the transaction and the expected gain or income
4. Officer review
The Assessing Officer examines your estimated income, past compliance and any outstanding tax demands, and may ask for more information
5. Certificate issued
If satisfied, the officer issues a certificate naming each payer, the rate and the maximum amount it covers. Payers can see and download it
6. Payers apply the rate
From the date of the certificate, each named payer deducts at the specified rate until the amount limit is reached or the tax year ends

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Application Form
body.textWithBlank: From tax year 2026-27, an application for a lower or nil TDS certificate under Section 395 is made in Form ___, which replaced Form 13.
body.explanation: Form 128 replaced Form 13. Certificates already issued under the old Section 197 for tax year 2026-27 continue to be honoured, but new applications use the new form.

events.title: Application filed
events.description: She files Form 128 with her estimate, naming all three hospitals and their TANs.

events.title: Waiting period
events.description: The hospitals keep deducting 10% while the application is processed. On about ₹8,00,000 of fees, that is ₹80,000 of TDS.

events.title: Certificate issued
events.description: The officer issues certificates at 6.5% for each hospital, with a cap on the amount each covers.

events.title: Lower rate applies
events.description: Each hospital deducts 6.5% until its cap is reached. If she earns more than estimated from one hospital, 10% resumes on the excess.

events.title: Return filed
events.description: The extra TDS from April and May, about ₹28,000, is adjusted in her return. The rest of the year's TDS already matches her tax.

body.title: Quick Check: Is the Certificate Retrospective?
body.question: Dr Farah's certificate is issued in early June. What happens to the 10% TDS the hospitals deducted in April and May?
options: The hospitals must refund the difference to her immediately
It stays deducted and she claims any excess in her return
The certificate automatically converts it to 6.5%
It is forfeited because she applied late
body.explanation: A certificate applies to payments made or credited after it is issued. TDS already deducted and deposited is not reversed. That is why it pays to apply at the very start of the tax year, or even before, and why any excess from the waiting period is recovered through the return.

body.text: An officer can refuse or reduce the relief. Unfiled returns, unpaid tax demands, income that looks under-estimated, or incomplete details of payers make a refusal more likely. And a certificate is capped: once a payer has paid you the amount it covers, normal TDS resumes, so estimate each payer's amount realistically.

body.title: Scenario: Mrs Iyer Applies for a Certificate
body.scenario: Mrs Iyer, the Dubai-based seller from Chapter 3, is selling her Navi Mumbai flat to Arvind for ₹90,00,000. She bought it in 2012 for ₹40,00,000. Arvind's chartered accountant says that without a certificate he will deduct TDS as though the whole sale price were long-term capital gain.
body.prompt: Roughly how much difference can a certificate make, and what should Mrs Iyer do? Ignore surcharge and any exemptions for simplicity.
body.modelAnswer: Payments to a non-resident attract TDS based on the tax the seller owes, and in the absence of a certificate buyers often apply the long-term capital gains rate of 12.5% plus cess to the entire price, since they cannot verify her cost. That is at least ₹90,00,000 × 12.5% × 1.04 = ₹11,70,000, before surcharge. Her actual gain is only ₹50,00,000, so tax on the gain is about ₹50,00,000 × 12.5% × 1.04 = ₹6,50,000. The difference of more than ₹5,20,000 would otherwise be refunded only after she files an Indian return. She should apply for a lower deduction certificate using Form 128 well before the sale date, with her purchase deed, cost details and any planned reinvestment that could exempt the gain. Once issued in Arvind's name, he deducts at the certified rate. If she plans to reinvest in a way that exempts the gain, the certificate may even be at a much lower rate or nil.

stats.label: Validity
stats.context: Per payer, up to the amount specified

body.title: Before You Apply Under Section 395
steps: Compare your expected TDS with your expected tax. A certificate is worth the effort only when the gap is significant
Check whether Form 121 is available first, since it is simpler
File all past returns and clear any outstanding tax demands
List every payer with its TAN and a realistic amount you expect from each
Apply at the start of the tax year, or well before a one-off transaction such as a property sale
Once issued, confirm each payer has applied the certificate, and track amounts against the cap

body.label: TRACES
body.description: The TDS Reconciliation Analysis and Correction Enabling System, used to apply for lower or nil deduction certificates and by payers to verify them.

cards.definition: Provision for certificates of lower or nil TDS, issued by the Assessing Officer. Formerly Section 197.
Application for a lower or nil TDS certificate. Replaced Form 13.
Directs a named payer to deduct at a specified lower rate, or nil, up to a specified amount for a tax year.
The maximum payment a certificate covers for a payer. Normal TDS resumes above it.
A certificate applies only from its date. Earlier TDS is adjusted through the return.
For eligible professionals, 50% of gross receipts treated as profit, often making 10% TDS on fees far higher than actual tax.

points: A Section 395 certificate (formerly Section 197) lets the Assessing Officer set a lower or nil TDS rate when your estimated income justifies it
Unlike Form 121, it is available to anyone, including non-residents, businesses and people whose tax is reduced but not nil
Apply online in Form 128 (formerly Form 13) with an income estimate, payer details and past returns, ideally before payments begin
Certificates name each payer, a rate and an amount cap, apply only from their date, and last for one tax year
Professionals with large gross receipts, people below 60 blocked by the Form 121 cap, and non-residents selling property benefit most
Clean compliance history and realistic estimates make approval far more likely

Names, amounts and rates are illustrative, and the property example ignores surcharge and exemptions. Procedures, form numbers and coverage reflect the position understood at the time of writing and can change.
